7.6 What to be careful about

  • \(\sigma\) is set, not fitted. The decay on school-to-school distance is fixed at 1. Fitting it as well as \(\delta\) on ten destination margins would be asking too much of the data.
  • Ten schools. Every statement here rests on ten points, and two tight pairs — Stringer with Varndean, Blatchington Mill with Hove Park — dominate the variation.
  • It is entangled with \(W_j\) and with \(\gamma\). The sum uses the attractiveness that was itself balanced with this term in place, and §6’s catchment term can do much of the same work.
  • Straight lines, not journeys. Two schools half a kilometre apart across a railway are as close, on this measure, as two half a kilometre apart on the same street.
  • Fitted on offers, not preferences. Unlike \(\gamma_h\), which was refitted against the catchment preference table, \(\delta\) was fitted against the offers made — and those are shaped by the ceiling as much as by choice.

7.7 Questions this raises

  1. Should \(\delta\) be refitted against preferences, as \(\gamma_h\) now is? That is the cleaner question, and this is the last term still fitted against the older target.
  2. Is the positive sign real, or is it standing in for something the model is missing — the faith schools’ city-wide draw, say, which happens to sit in the crowded middle of the city?
  3. Would a nested form — choose an area, then a school within it — represent the paired catchments better than an exponent on clustering does?

8 \(A_i\): the balancing factor

8.1 What it is

\(A_i\) is not a thing anyone chooses or observes. It is whatever number makes each neighbourhood’s row of the matrix add up to the children who live there:

\[\sum_j T_{ij}^{\,y} = O_i^{\,y} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A_i^{\,y} \;=\; \frac{1}{\sum_k W_k\, c_{ik}^{-\beta}\, e^{\gamma_{h(i)}\mathbb{1}[\cdot]}\, C_k^{\delta}}\]

Call the denominator the neighbourhood’s total pull: everything the city offers it, discounted by how hard each school is to reach. \(A_i\) is its reciprocal, and the model then divides the children of \(i\) between schools in proportion to each school’s share of that total:

\[T_{ij} \;=\; O_i \times \frac{\text{pull}_{ij}}{\sum_k \text{pull}_{ik}}\]

This is what “production-constrained” means, and it is the single strongest assumption in the model. Every child is placed somewhere. Demand cannot leak away, and it cannot grow because the city got better: if every school became less attractive tomorrow, \(A_i\) would simply rise to compensate and exactly the same children would be distributed in exactly the same proportions.

8.2 Computed per population, not per zone

One subtlety: the model does not balance over zones but over origin-populations. In the two paired catchments some families will take one of the pair but not the other, so a zone there carries up to three populations with different choice sets, each balanced on its own.

Show code 
d_ai %>% distinct(orig, pop, zone) %>%
  count(pop, name = "Origins") %>%
  mutate(Population = ifelse(pop == "either", "Everyone else", pop)) %>%
  select(Population, Origins) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lr")
The origin-populations the model balances over. Each is a group of children with its own choice set, and therefore its own balancing factor.
Population Origins
Everyone else 195
only Blatchington Mill School 61
only Dorothy Stringer School 58
only Hove Park School 61
only Varndean School 58

That is 433 origins over 195 zones, and it matters because a child who would not take Varndean must have Varndean out of the denominator, not merely low in it. Otherwise refusing them at Dorothy Stringer would send them next door.

The range is extreme — from 24 to 3156 on an index with the median at 100 — and most of it is the catchment term compounding with distance. A neighbourhood between Dorothy Stringer and Varndean has two schools it can walk to and the catchment bonus on both. A neighbourhood in Ovingdean has one school within easy reach, with the lowest \(W_j\) in the city.

For the far east of the city the denominator also contains schools outside it. In a typical Longhill-catchment neighbourhood they are 15.3% of the total pull, and they are under 2.7% everywhere west of Brighton Aldridge’s.

Read the two tables side by side and the model’s behaviour is visible in one page. In the first, 95% of the row goes to the two catchment schools before anything else is considered. NoteThe balancing factor is not the accessibility index, but it is close

The strategic view reports an accessibility index for each neighbourhood. That is the same sum with the behavioural terms stripped out — attractiveness and journey time only, no catchment bonus, no competition term, city schools alone. The two rank neighbourhoods similarly but not identically (Spearman \(\rho = 0.82\)), and the difference is mostly the catchment term: it rewards the neighbourhoods that are already close to a wanted school.

8.5 Where it sits in the sequence

\(A_i\) is applied to the uncapped pull, before any admission number is consulted. The model first works out what families want, and only then rations it (§9), re-offering the children who are refused (§10).

The constraint survives that. After the ceiling and the re-offering, the row still sums to the children who live there — nobody is lost in rationing, they are only placed elsewhere:

8.6 What to be careful about

  • No demand response. Because the row is fixed at \(O_i\), nothing the model does can make families leave the state system, home-school, move house, or appear from elsewhere. A scenario that makes every school worse produces the same 2,267 placements as one that makes every school better. Where a scenario would plausibly change how many families opt out, the model will not show it, and §2’s state-sector share is the only place that quantity lives.
  • Substitution is proportional. Close a school, and the children who wanted it are redistributed among the others in proportion to those schools’ existing pull for that neighbourhood — the classic independence-of-irrelevant-alternatives behaviour. The exclusivity populations are a patch on exactly this, for the one case where it is known to be wrong.
  • It absorbs everything the model does not contain. Any systematic pull the equation misses is silently rescaled away by \(A_i\) rather than showing up as a residual. A model that fits well at the school level can still be wrong about why.
  • It is recomputed in every run. Change a year, a slider, a boundary or a school’s existence and the denominator changes for every affected neighbourhood. \(A_i\) is never carried over between runs.

8.7 Questions this raises

  1. Should the state-sector share respond to the scenario rather than being fixed in \(O_i\) — a doubly-constrained or elastic form?
  2. Should the choice set be truncated — some neighbourhoods carry fourteen destinations when families realistically consider three or four?
  3. Are the exclusivity populations the right patch for proportional substitution, or should the whole thing be nested?

9 The admission-number ceiling

9.1 What happens after the matrix

Sections 2 to 8 produce \(T_{ij}\): how many children in each neighbourhood want each school as their first choice. Nothing in that calculation knows how many places a school has. The city’s demand, laid against the admission numbers and against what families actually named, does not fit:

  theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "horizontal",
        plot.title.position = "plot") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), shape = guide_legend(nrow = 2))

The model’s demand is a first choice, and a first choice is not the whole story. The council runs an equal-preference system: every school a family names is considered on the same footing, and a family is offered the highest-ranked of its schools where it qualifies. So a school can be named first by fewer families than it holds and still refuse some of them. Dorothy Stringer is the clearest case. In 2026 301 families put it first, against 330 places, and 412 more put it second. Only 264 of those who put it first were offered it: the rest of its places went to families with a higher priority who had ranked it second or third.

The model represents that in two places rather than in the demand itself. Families in the two paired catchments are treated as content with either school unless they are among the few who would take only one (3% would take only Stringer and 6% only Varndean, §8), and a family refused at one school of a pair is offered the other before anywhere else (§10). Counting those families, the model’s demand for Stringer as a first choice or as the partner of a first choice at Varndean is 552, against the 713 families who named it first or second.

The ceiling is where the model stops being about preferences and starts being about administration. It is also where most of the fit comes from: §7 showed that without it the behavioural terms explain almost nothing.

9.2 Two ceilings

The simulator carries both, and which one is in force is a setting.

The proportional ceiling (rule = "published") cuts every applicant to an oversubscribed school back by the same share. That is the average outcome of a single lottery over everyone who applied, and it is what the published model used before the council’s priorities were added.

The tiered ceiling (rule = "priorities") fills each community school’s places in the council’s own order, and runs a proportional cut only within a tier — which is what a lottery inside a priority averages to. Every number in this guide and in the strategic view uses this one.

Show code 
tibble::tribble(
  ~Priority, ~`Who`, ~`Ceiling on the tier`,
  "1–3", "Looked-after children, SEN and exceptional need, siblings",
  "not separable in zone-level flows — see below",
  "4", "Children eligible for free school meals living in the catchment",
  sprintf("with 5, up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$fsm_cap_share),
  "5", "Children eligible for free school meals living elsewhere",
  sprintf("with 4, up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$fsm_cap_share),
  "6", "Children from a single-school catchment applying outside it",
  sprintf("up to %.0f%% of the admission number", 100 * rl$p6_share),
  "7", "Children living in the catchment", "whatever is left",
  "8", "Everyone else", "whatever is left after that") %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lll")
The council’s oversubscription priorities as the model applies them at the six community schools. Academies and faith schools keep the proportional ceiling: their criteria are not in any published data.
Priority Who Ceiling on the tier
1–3 Looked-after children, SEN and exceptional need, siblings not separable in zone-level flows — see below
4 Children eligible for free school meals living in the catchment with 5, up to 30% of the admission number
5 Children eligible for free school meals living elsewhere with 4, up to 30% of the admission number
6 Children from a single-school catchment applying outside it up to 5% of the admission number
7 Children living in the catchment whatever is left
8 Everyone else whatever is left after that

A child who misses a capped tier drops to the one below: an FSM child in the catchment falls to 7, an FSM child from elsewhere to 6 if they qualify and 8 if not, a priority-6 child to 8. Nobody is removed from the queue by missing a tier.

NoteWhat the model cannot see: priorities 1 to 3

Looked-after children, children with SEN or exceptional need, and siblings cannot be told apart in flows between neighbourhoods and schools — nothing in the published data says which children have a sibling already at a school. Most siblings live in the catchment, so they sit inside tier 7, and the comparison below folds the council’s published priority 3 into tier 7 for that reason.

The tie-break inside each priority is a random draw, not distance: the council’s published admission arrangements break ties by random allocation. That is what makes a proportional cut within a tier the right average.

9.3 Who counts as FSM

The tiers need to know how many children in each neighbourhood are eligible for free school meals. The model has no pupil records, so it uses the neighbourhood’s IDACI score scaled by a single number:

\[\text{FSM share of zone } i \;=\; \min\!\left(1.29 \times \text{IDACI}_i,\; 0.95\right)\]

That multiplier is not chosen. It is solved for, so that the FSM-priority places the model gives at the three rationing schools total the 192 the council actually made in 2026. It puts 20% of the city’s Year 7 children in the FSM group. It is a calibrated quantity, not a measured one, and it inherits whatever IDACI gets wrong about who is eligible where.

9.4 Against the published outturn

The council publishes, for the three schools that actually rationed in 2026, how many offers went out under each priority. The model was fitted to the total of tiers 4 and 5 only; everything else in this chart is free.

Show code 
tier_cmp %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(c(modelled, observed), names_to = "src", values_to = "n") %>%
  mutate(src = factor(src, c("observed", "modelled"), c("Council", "Model")),
         tier = factor(tier, c("FSM (4, 5)", "Single-school catchment (6)",
                               "In catchment, siblings included (3, 7)",
                               "Everyone else (8)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(n, forcats::fct_rev(tier), fill = src)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.7), width = 0.65) +
  facet_wrap(~ School, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Council = "#1f3b57", Model = "#d95f02"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Offers", y = NULL,
       title = "The ceiling, tier by tier, against what the council did",
       subtitle = "2026 entry. The council's priorities 0 to 2 are left out; the model cannot separate them from the tiers it has") +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "top",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))

The catchment tier is close at all three schools, and priority 6 is almost exact — it is capped at 5% of the admission number and the model fills the cap, as the council did. The FSM tiers are the weak point: the model gives Varndean the full 30% and the council gave it fewer, because an FSM child with a sibling at the school is admitted under priority 3 and never reaches the FSM tier at all. The three-school total is right by construction; the split between them is the model’s own, and it is too generous where siblings are most common.

54 offers across the three schools went to looked-after children, children with SEN and exceptional need. The model places those children somewhere — it just cannot tell you that this is why.

Notice Dorothy Stringer and Blatchington Mill. Both are the first choice of fewer children than they have places for, and both finish full. 9.7 What to be careful about

  • It is a mean, not a draw. Every number here is the average outcome of the lottery, so no scenario in this work shows the spread. The variance of a real allocation round is not modelled.
  • Admission numbers are the published ones, not the numbers a school could take. Where a school has taken over its admission number in the past, the model will not.
  • Only community schools get the tiers. The two academy trusts and the two faith schools keep the proportional cut, so their intakes carry no priority structure at all — and Cardinal Newman has the largest admission number in the city.
  • The FSM group is a neighbourhood share, not a child. A zone contributes its IDACI-scaled fraction to the FSM tiers of every school it sends children to. That is a reasonable average and a poor description of any individual.
  • Siblings are inside the catchment tier, which makes the FSM tiers too large at the schools where siblings are most numerous.

9.8 Questions this raises

  1. Would a sibling term be estimable from the published data — last year’s intake by catchment, scaled by an average family size?
  2. Should the model run the lottery rather than average it, so the uncertainty in a marginal neighbourhood’s outcome is visible?
  3. Should the academies’ and faith schools’ own criteria be modelled from their published admission policies rather than left proportional?

10 Re-offering the children who are refused

10.1 Why a proportional cut is not enough

The ceiling in §9 tells each full school how many of its applicants it can take. It does not say what happens to the rest. Left there, the production constraint of §8 would rescale each neighbourhood’s remaining flows to place its children — which spreads a child refused at Varndean across every other school in proportion to how much they wanted each one first.

That is not what happens. A family refused at Varndean who would also take Dorothy Stringer gets Dorothy Stringer. A family refused at Cardinal Newman goes where families in their part of the city put their second preference. So refused demand is re-offered explicitly, in two steps, and only ever to schools that still have room.

10.2 Step one: the partner school

In the two paired catchments — Stringer with Varndean, Hove Park with Blatchington Mill — a family who would take either school and is refused at one is offered the other before anything else is considered.

Show code 
tibble(key = names(partner_ov), partner = unname(partner_ov)) %>%
  tidyr::separate(key, c("Catchment", "Refused at"), sep = " ", extra = "merge") %>%
  transmute(Catchment = catch_lab(Catchment),
            `Refused at` = short_sch(`Refused at`),
            `Offered instead` = short_sch(partner)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lll")
The partner map. It follows the family’s own catchment, so it holds under any boundary design.
Catchment Refused at Offered instead
Hove Park / Blatchington Mill Hove Park Blatchington Mill
Hove Park / Blatchington Mill Blatchington Mill Hove Park
Varndean / Dorothy Stringer Dorothy Stringer Varndean
Varndean / Dorothy Stringer Varndean Dorothy Stringer

The families who would take only one of the pair are excluded from this step: they are carried as populations of their own (§8), and a child who would not take Stringer is never sent there.

10.3 Step two: the second preferences of their catchment

Everything else is shared among the schools with room, in proportion to the second preferences families in that home catchment actually gave. That is the council’s catchment preference table, pooled over 3 rounds, normalised within each catchment:

Show code 
kern_tbl %>%
  group_by(catchment) %>% slice_max(share, n = 3) %>% ungroup() %>%
  transmute(Catchment = catch_lab(catchment),
            School = short_sch(school),
            `Share of the catchment's second preferences` = fmt_pct(100 * share)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "llr")
The three schools each catchment’s families most often name second. Sixty numbers in all — six catchments by ten schools.
Catchment School Share of the catchment’s second preferences
BACA (Brighton Aldridge) Varndean 29%
BACA (Brighton Aldridge) Patcham 26%
BACA (Brighton Aldridge) Dorothy Stringer 22%
Varndean / Dorothy Stringer Dorothy Stringer 55%
Varndean / Dorothy Stringer Varndean 32%
Varndean / Dorothy Stringer Cardinal Newman 6%
Hove Park / Blatchington Mill Blatchington Mill 31%
Hove Park / Blatchington Mill Hove Park 25%
Hove Park / Blatchington Mill King’s 21%
Longhill Varndean 24%
Longhill Dorothy Stringer 21%
Longhill Longhill 17%
PACA (Portslade Aldridge) Hove Park 30%
PACA (Portslade Aldridge) King’s 27%
PACA (Portslade Aldridge) Blatchington Mill 18%
Patcham Varndean 42%
Patcham Dorothy Stringer 31%
Patcham Patcham 14%

A catchment-level table would send every neighbourhood in Longhill’s catchment the same way, so it is modulated by where the neighbourhood actually is. Each neighbourhood’s weight on school \(j\) is

\[b_{ij} \;=\; k_{h(i),j} \times \frac{u_{ij}}{\bar u_{h(i),j}}\]

where \(u_{ij}\) is the share of \(i\)’s children the model sent to \(j\) before rationing and \(\bar u\) is the average of that share across the catchment. A neighbourhood at the Patcham end of Varndean’s catchment therefore sends more of its overflow to Patcham than one at the other end, without anyone having to write that rule down.

NoteWhen a school has moved

The second preferences in the table were given with the schools where they stand today. If a run moves one — Longhill to Elm Grove — the comparison \(u/\bar u\) is made against the flows at today’s sites, so a catchment that the move brings a school nearer to sends it more of its overflow. Without that correction the kernel would be read against a city the families answering it never saw. With no move, the two are the same flow and nothing changes.

10.4 What it does in 2026

Show code 
flows_plot <- A_ov %>%
  group_by(from = short_sch(from), to = short_sch(to), route) %>%
  summarise(n = sum(n), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n > 0.5) %>%
  mutate(from = forcats::fct_reorder(from, n, sum),
         to = forcats::fct_reorder(to, n, sum))
ggplot(flows_plot, aes(n, from, fill = to)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ route, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2", name = "Offered instead") +
  labs(x = "Children", y = "Refused at",
       title = sprintf("%.0f children are re-offered somewhere else",
                       sum(A_ov$n)),
       subtitle = sprintf("2026 entry, current catchment map. %.0f take the partner school, %.0f follow second preferences",
                          route_n("Partner school"), route_n("Second preferences"))) +
  theme_bh() +
  theme(legend.position = "right",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))

The cascade runs 3 rounds, refusing 257, then 25, then nobody. Re-offered demand can overfill a school with a little room left, so the next round cuts it back and re-offers the excess again; the totals fall away quickly because each round has less to place and fewer schools to place it in.

Two things in that chart are worth stating plainly. The largest single movement in the city is Varndean to Dorothy Stringer (86 children by both routes together), which is why Stringer finishes full despite being wanted first by fewer children than it has places for. And the schools receiving the overflow are, in order, Dorothy Stringer, Blatchington Mill, Hove Park — the schools with room, not the schools nearest the refusal.

10.5 This is where displacement comes from

The strategic view’s displacement measure is the difference between the two quantities this section connects: what a neighbourhood’s children wanted, and what they were offered. A child who is counted as displaced is a child who appears somewhere in the chart above.

Show code 
d_ai %>%
  mutate(lost = pmax(wanted - flow, 0)) %>%
  group_by(zone) %>%
  summarise(Oi = first(Oi), catchment = first(catchment),
            lost = sum(lost), .groups = "drop") %>%
  slice_max(lost, n = 6) %>%
  transmute(Neighbourhood = sub("[|].*$", "", zone),
            Catchment = catch_lab(catchment),
            `Children` = sprintf("%.0f", Oi),
            `Refused their first choice` = sprintf("%.0f", lost),
            `Share` = fmt_pct(100 * lost / Oi)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "llrrr")

10.7 What to be careful about

  • The kernel is fixed, and it is pre-2024. The second preferences come from the catchment table the council published for the old boundaries. Under a redrawn map the model still uses them, modulated by proximity but not re-estimated.
  • Second preferences are not a preference for a school with room. The table records what families named when the school they wanted was still possible. A family whose second choice is also full is handled by the next round, which is a reasonable mechanism but not an observed one.
  • Overflow stays in the city. The kernel has entries for the ten city schools only, so a refused child is never re-offered a school outside Brighton and Hove — although out-of-city schools are in the choice set at the first stage (§8) and take 50 children in 2026 that way.
  • It is demand, not children. Every quantity here is a fraction of a neighbourhood’s cohort, so “68 children take the partner school” means 68 children’s worth of demand spread over many neighbourhoods.
  • Refusal has no cost. A family refused twice is no less likely to be placed than one refused once, and nothing in the model records how far down their own list a child ends up.

10.8 Questions this raises

  1. Should the kernel be re-estimated for a redrawn map, or is the proximity modulation enough?
  2. Should third preferences enter, rather than the cascade re-using second preferences in every round?
  3. Should a refused child be allowed out of the city, as they can be at the first stage?

11 The algorithm, end to end

Sections 2 to 10 take the model apart a term at a time. This one puts it back together in the order the code actually executes it, and shows where each of the simulator’s controls attaches — because every control does its work by changing an input to one of these steps and making the whole sequence run again.

11.1 What each control changes, and what it makes the model redo

Show code

Every control in the simulator, the step it attaches to, and what has to be recomputed when it moves.
Control What it sets Recomputed
Entry year the cohort index that scales every zone’s \(O_i\) (§2.7) everything: the rows change size, so the ceiling binds differently
Catchment map which catchment each zone and each school belongs to (§6) the catchment indicator, the priority-6 rule, and which school is a family’s partner in the cascade

When a school is full proportional ceiling or the council’s tiers, the priority-6 share, and whether the FSM priority applies (§9) the ceiling and the cascade, not the demand that goes into them

11.2 What a control never changes

This is the important half of the picture. No control in the simulator moves a fitted parameter. The things estimated in §3 and §5 to §7 — the balanced attractiveness, \(\beta\), each catchment’s \(\gamma_h\), \(\delta\) and \(\sigma\) — are fixed when the input bundle is built, and a run reads them. So does the second-preference kernel (§10), the disadvantage pull \(\lambda_j\) (§12), and the two routed cost tables, which are far too slow to build inside a run.

That division is what the sliders mean. The catchment slider does not re-estimate how much families follow their catchment; it multiplies the estimate by a number you choose, and the honest reading of any slider position other than 1 is “what if this were different”, never “this is what it would be”.

11.3 Where the loops are

Both are in the rationing: one loop, and a fixed sequence inside it.

The outer loop is the one drawn above: cut every over-subscribed school back to its admission number, re-offer the children refused, which may overfill a school that had a little room, so cut again. In 2026 it takes 3 passes (257, then 25 children refused, then none). It stops when nothing is refused or no school has room left; children who cannot be placed anywhere stay unplaced rather than being forced over an admission number.

The sequence inside it is the tier cascade within a single pass: a child who misses a capped tier at a community school drops into the next tier down (§9), in a fixed order rather than by iterating, and the two groups — FSM-eligible and everyone else — are carried through it separately so each places its own children.

A third loop, outside the model, sits in the disadvantage layer (§12): it shares each neighbourhood’s disadvantaged children over the flows it has already produced, spilling any excess where a school would otherwise be sent more disadvantaged children than children.

11.4 Why it recomputes rather than updates

Everything above takes about 0.07 seconds for the model and another 0.06 for all of the outcome measures, on 5,824 zone-school rows. That is fast enough that the simulator does not attempt to update anything incrementally: every change to any control re-runs the whole sequence from step 1. Nothing is cached between runs, so nothing can be stale, and two runs with identical settings are identical to the last decimal place.

It also means the comparisons the simulator shows — this scenario against the baseline, or a school’s fill now against 2030 — are two complete runs compared afterwards, not one run adjusted.

12 Who is disadvantaged, and where they go

Everything up to here places children. The strategic view’s integration measures need to know which children: how the city’s disadvantaged Year 7 cohort is spread across the ten schools, how far those children travel, and what a scenario does to both. That is a layer on top of the model, and this section sets it out because every segregation number in this work depends on it.

12.1 The measure that was not good enough

The first version of this work measured a school’s intake by the neighbourhoods its children came from: sum the flows, weight by each neighbourhood’s deprivation, done. It is the natural thing to do with a spatial interaction model, and it is wrong.

Show code 
dis_fit %>%
  select(short, Neighbourhood = neighbourhood, Published = target) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-short, names_to = "what", values_to = "share") %>%
  mutate(what = factor(what, c("Neighbourhood", "Published")),
         short = forcats::fct_reorder(short, share, max)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(share, short, group = short)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = what), size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Neighbourhood = "#d95f02", Published = "#1f3b57"),
                      name = NULL,
                      labels = c("Measured by the neighbourhoods children come from",
                                 "What the school actually has")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
       title = "Within a mixed neighbourhood, families do not choose alike",
       subtitle = "Disadvantaged share of the intake, ten city schools") +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical",
                     legend.justification = "left")

Longhill is the clearest case: the neighbourhoods its children come from are 19% disadvantaged, and the school is 49%. Its catchment contains Rottingdean and Ovingdean as well as Whitehawk, and the two do not send their children to the same school. A measure that cannot see inside a neighbourhood cannot see that, and a segregation index built on it is measuring residential segregation with a school label attached.

12.2 So the children are placed explicitly

Two ingredients, and one rule.

Each neighbourhood has a disadvantaged share. As in §9, it is the IDACI score scaled by a single constant, capped at 95%:

\[\text{disadvantaged share of zone } i \;=\; \min\!\left(1.75 \times \text{IDACI}_i,\; 0.95\right)\]

Each school has a pull. \(\lambda_j\) is how much more, or less, likely a disadvantaged child is to end up at school \(j\) than the rest of the children in the same flow. It is one number per school, and it is fitted.

The rule. Within each origin-population, the neighbourhood’s disadvantaged children are shared over the schools that neighbourhood’s children attend, in proportion to \(T_{ij}\lambda_j\), and never more than \(T_{ij}\) itself — a school cannot be sent more disadvantaged children than it is sent children. Where that cap binds, the excess spills to the other schools in the row and the sharing repeats.

ImportantThe flows themselves are never touched

This layer labels children inside flows the model has already produced; it does not move anybody. Disadvantage plays no part in where the model sends children, in the ceiling, or in the re-offering. That is a deliberate separation — the places are decided by preference, distance and admission rules, and the disadvantage measure then reads off who is in them — but it does mean the model cannot represent a family’s circumstances changing what they ask for.

12.3 What \(\lambda\) is fitted to

Show code 
dis_fit %>%
  arrange(desc(target)) %>%
  transmute(School = short,
            `Whole school, published` = fmt_pct(100 * published),
            `Year 7, 2026` = ifelse(is.na(year7_fsm), "—", fmt_pct(100 * year7_fsm)),
            `Fitted to` = fmt_pct(100 * target),
            `Modelled` = fmt_pct(100 * modelled),
            `$\\lambda_j$` = sprintf("%.2f", lambda)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrr")
The target for each school, and the pull that reproduces it. Community schools are fitted to their September 2026 Year 7 free-school-meal offers; the academies and the faith schools have no published Year 7 figure, so they are fitted to their whole-school disadvantaged share.
School Whole school, published Year 7, 2026 Fitted to Modelled \(\lambda_j\)
Longhill 34% 49% 49% 49% 5.95
Brighton Aldridge 48% — 48% 48% 0.87
Hove Park 32% 35% 35% 35% 1.42
Varndean 23% 30% 30% 30% 0.68
Portslade Aldridge 28% — 28% 28% 0.75
Patcham 22% 27% 27% 27% 1.16
Dorothy Stringer 19% 25% 25% 25% 0.71
Blatchington Mill 17% 22% 22% 22% 1.02
Cardinal Newman 17% — 17% 17% 0.62
King’s 16% — 16% 16% 0.51

Three things in that table need saying.

The Year 7 figures are higher than the whole-school ones at the community schools. That is the free-school-meal admission priority working: it began with the September 2025 round, so a school’s current Year 7 is more disadvantaged than its Years 8 to 11. Fitting to the whole-school figure would have calibrated the model to the policy’s absence. This is the lag correction, and it is the reason the targets are mixed.

The academies and faith schools are fitted to the wrong vintage, for want of a right one. No Year 7 breakdown is published for them. Their targets are the Department for Education’s three-year mean, so if their Year 7 intakes have moved as the community schools’ have, the model will not know.

Longhill’s \(\lambda\) is extreme. 5.9 against about 1 for a school taking its fair share. It has to be: the school is 49% disadvantaged on an intake of only 88 children drawn from neighbourhoods that are, on the model’s own numbers, much less disadvantaged than that. A large \(\lambda\) on a small intake is a fragile thing, and it is the single number the segregation results are most sensitive to.

12.3.1 Why it is extreme: Longhill was fitted across a boundary change

There is a reason this one number is so far from the others, and it is not entirely behavioural. Longhill’s catchment changed between the rounds the model is fitted to and the round it is calibrated on.

Until the 2026 entry year, Whitehawk was in Longhill’s catchment. The council consulted from October 2024, determined the new arrangements in March 2025, and they governed applications made in the autumn of 2025 — so September 2026 was the first intake under the map that moved Whitehawk out. That is the round \(\lambda\) is fitted to.

The model does represent the change. On the pre-2024 map it sends 17 of Whitehawk’s children to Longhill; on today’s map, 0. Geography alone puts Longhill at 30% disadvantaged under the old map and 23% under today’s. What it was actually offered in September 2026 was 49%.

So the pull has to be enormous to close a gap that the boundary change opened. Fitted three ways, the same school gives:

Show code 
tibble::tibble(
  `Fitted to` = c("The published three-year share, on the pre-2024 map",
                  "The published three-year share, on today's map",
                  "The September 2026 Year 7 offers, on today's map (adopted)"),
  Target = c(fmt_pct(100 * dfl$published), fmt_pct(100 * dfl$published),
             fmt_pct(100 * dfl$target)),
  `$\\lambda$` = sprintf("%.2f", c(dfl$lambda_pre, dfl$lambda_today_map, dfl$lambda))) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrr")
Longhill’s fitted pull on disadvantaged children, against three different targets and maps.
Fitted to Target \(\lambda\)
The published three-year share, on the pre-2024 map 34% 1.31
The published three-year share, on today’s map 34% 2.26
The September 2026 Year 7 offers, on today’s map (adopted) 49% 5.95

Read that table slowly. Under the old map, with the old target, Longhill’s pull was 1.31 — barely above its fair share. Geography did nearly all the work, because Whitehawk was in the catchment. Take Whitehawk out and fit to the first cohort admitted without it, and the pull has to do the work instead.

The awkward fact is that the first intake under the new map was the most disadvantaged on record. If Whitehawk’s families had simply followed the boundary, Longhill’s share should have fallen. It rose. Longhill is well under its admission number, so a family living outside its catchment who names it is admitted anyway — and on these figures a good many still did. The catchment term suppresses that demand harder than the first year’s offers suggest it should, and \(\lambda\) quietly makes up the difference.

That matters because \(\lambda\) is then carried forward unchanged to 2035. Doing so assumes the transition never completes. Carrying the pre-change pulls forward instead assumes the opposite — that families follow the map at once. The two bracket the answer:

Show code 
tibble::tibble(
  Assumption = c("Pulls fitted to the 2026 offers (as published here)",
                 "Pulls fitted before the boundary change"),
  `Longhill's intake` = sprintf("%.0f", c(wh_n30$intake, wh_a30$intake)),
  `Disadvantaged` = c(fmt_pct(100 * wh_n30$dep), fmt_pct(100 * wh_a30$dep)),
  `Segregation index` = sprintf("%.3f", c(wh_n30$gorard, wh_a30$gorard))) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrr")
Longhill in 2030 under the two assumptions, with the city’s segregation index beside it.
Assumption Longhill’s intake Disadvantaged Segregation index
Pulls fitted to the 2026 offers (as published here) 70 50% 0.106
Pulls fitted before the boundary change 70 25% 0.121

A school that is half disadvantaged or a quarter disadvantaged is not a detail, and the difference in the city’s segregation index, 0.015, is an appreciable fraction of the spread across all the options in the strategic view. Every figure in these documents uses the first assumption, which is the conservative one for any argument that the city is segregated, and the wrong one if Whitehawk’s families are still in the process of moving.

There is a second reading worth holding alongside the first, and it points the other way. Longhill’s intake has collapsed to 88 children. The families still choosing it may be disproportionately deprived whatever the map says, because the others have the means and the inclination to go elsewhere. That is sorting, and it would persist. Nothing here separates the two, and only one thing will: the September 2027 and 2028 factsheets. If Longhill’s free school meal share falls back towards a third, the boundary explanation was right and \(\lambda\) is overstated. If it stays near a half, the sorting explanation was right and \(\lambda\) is measuring something real.

Show code

  mutate(short = forcats::fct_reorder(short, lambda),
         side = lambda >= 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(lambda, short, fill = side)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", lambda)), hjust = -0.15,
            size = 3.1, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1f3b57", `TRUE` = "#d95f02"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.12))) +

       subtitle = "Fitted pull on disadvantaged children, 2026, today's map and admission rules") +

The integration measures the strategic view reports, for the baseline run.
Measure Value What it is
Gorard segregation index 0.116 half the sum of each school’s share of the city’s disadvantaged children less its share of all of them; 0 is an even spread
Most and least disadvantaged intake 49% and 16% the ends of the same distribution

Every scenario in the strategic view is scored on the first and the third of those. A boundary redraw, a closure, a change to admission priorities: what moves is which schools the flows go to, and this layer turns that into a segregation number.

WarningThis measure has changed sign more than once

The direction of a headline finding — whether moving Longhill’s catchment out of Whitehawk raises or lowers segregation — has changed three times during this work, and every change came from a correction to measurement, not to the scenario:

  1. on the neighbourhood measure, it lowered segregation;
  2. on the whole-school fit against today’s map, it raised it;
  3. fitted on the map in force before the change, it was flat;
  4. on Year 7 offers with the corrected neighbourhood weighting, it raises it again.

The scenario never moved. That is a warning about how much weight a single segregation index can carry, and it is why the strategic view reports the direction with the calibration it depends on stated alongside.

12.6 What to be careful about

  • Two different disadvantage scalings live in this model, and they are not a mistake. §9’s 1.29 × IDACI is the group with current free-school-meal eligibility, because that is who the admission priority applies to. This section’s 1.75 × IDACI is the broader disadvantaged group — free school meals at any point in six years, plus looked-after children — because that is what the published school-level figures count. They answer different questions and are calibrated to different targets.
  • \(\lambda\) is a summary of everything not modelled. Sibling patterns, transport cost, appeals, the confidence to name an over-subscribed school first: all of it is inside one number per school.
  • It is fitted on one year. A single admissions round, on the current map, under the current rules.
  • A higher index is not a measured harm. The Gorard index describes how unevenly disadvantaged children are spread, which is what the council’s policy aim is framed around. It says nothing about their results. The national evidence in How to Pull the Right Lever is that disadvantaged pupils do slightly better, not worse, in schools with more of them once absence and prior attainment are allowed for, and the strategic view sets out what that means for the options (the strategic view).
  • A scenario’s segregation number is only as good as \(\lambda\). The model holds the pull fixed while it moves boundaries and schools, which assumes a school’s relationship with disadvantaged families travels with it. For a relocation like Elm Grove that is a strong assumption and it is impossible to test from published data.

12.7 Questions this raises

  1. Should \(\lambda\) be modelled rather than fitted — as a function of distance, catchment and school characteristics — so it can respond to a scenario instead of being carried through it?
  2. Should the disadvantage layer feed back into the flows, so that a family’s circumstances change what they ask for as well as what they get?
  3. Is the Gorard index the right summary, given how much of the movement above came from re-measurement rather than from the system changing?

13 From intakes to money

The strategic view’s money section argues that the city’s schools are already spending their reserves and that small schools are the most exposed. The simulator turns that into a number for every run: given the intakes a configuration produces, where does each school’s budget land? This section is the arithmetic behind that number, and it is deliberately simple — simple enough to be done by hand for any one school.

13.1 What each school starts from

Show code 
fin %>%
  arrange(short) %>%
  transmute(School = short,
            `Funded roll` = fmt_n(funded_roll),
            `Pupil-led rate` = sprintf("£%s", fmt_n(marginal_pp)),
            `Fixed funding` = gbp_k(fixed),
            Income = sprintf("£%.1fm", income / 1e6),
            `In-year balance` = gbp_k(balance),
            Reserve = gbp_k(reserve),
            `Accounts year` = year_label) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrrl")
What the money calculation starts from. Rolls and funding rates are from the DfE’s school-level funding statistics for 2025–26; income, reserve and in-year balance are each school’s latest published return.
School Funded roll Pupil-led rate Fixed funding Income In-year balance Reserve Accounts year
Blatchington Mill 1,626 £6,570 £428k £12.4m −£246k £492k 2024-25
Brighton Aldridge 700 £7,889 £152k £7.2m £383k £1k 2023-24
Cardinal Newman 1,851 £6,707 £236k £17.6m −£1,740k −£1,777k 2024-25
Dorothy Stringer 1,643 £6,744 £566k £13.2m £37k £831k 2024-25
Hove Park 949 £7,331 £527k £9.6m −£546k −£1,052k 2024-25
King’s 867 £6,548 £152k £6.5m £795k £1,011k 2023-24
Longhill 719 £7,440 £342k £7.5m −£168k £531k 2024-25
Patcham 1,107 £6,675 £444k £9.0m £371k −£82k 2024-25
Portslade Aldridge 950 £7,026 £152k £7.7m £791k £534k 2023-24
Varndean 1,493 £6,643 £511k £12.2m −£151k £662k 2024-25
  • The funded roll is the pupil count the school’s 2025–26 schools block allocation was calculated on. The schools block funds Years 7 to 11 only, so a sixth form is not in it.
  • The pupil-led rate is what one more pupil in Years 7 to 11 brings in. It is the school’s whole allocation less the parts that do not depend on pupil numbers — the lump sum, and where they apply, split site, rates, PFI and exceptional factors — divided by the funded roll. Those fixed parts are why a small school receives more per pupil and loses less per pupil than the average suggests.
  • Income, reserve and in-year balance come from each school’s own accounts: the Consistent Financial Reporting return for maintained schools (to 31 March) and the Academies Accounts Return for the three academies (to 31 August). The academies’ latest published year is therefore a year behind the others, which the table shows rather than hides.

13.2 The calculation

For each school, in a run:

\[\text{roll}_j = 5 \times \text{intake}_j\]

\[\Delta\text{funding}_j = (\text{roll}_j - \text{funded roll}_j) \times \text{pupil-led rate}_j\]

\[\text{annual balance}_j = \text{in-year balance}_j + \Delta\text{funding}_j \times (1 - s)\]

\[\text{years of reserve}_j = \frac{\text{reserve}_j}{-\,\text{annual balance}_j}\quad\text{when the balance is negative}\]

Three choices are built into those four lines.

The roll is a steady state. Five year groups at this run’s intake is the roll the school converges on if the configuration holds for five years — not the roll next September. A school whose intake falls today feels a fifth of the loss next year and all of it in year five.

Today’s in-year balance is carried forward. A school that ran a deficit in its latest accounts is assumed to keep running it, before any change in pupils. That is the least-assumption starting point, and it means a single unusual year in a school’s accounts carries straight through.

\(s\) is how much of the lost funding the school can take out of its costs. A school that loses £100k of funding and cuts £75k of spending ends £25k worse off. The simulator uses \(s = 0.75\), the middle of the three assumptions in the strategic view (90%, 75% and 50%). It is symmetric: a school that gains pupils is assumed to spend three quarters of the new money.

13.3 Worked example: Longhill

Longhill’s funded roll is 719. The model gives it an intake of 88 in 2026, so the steady-state roll is 442 — 277 fewer pupils. At its pupil-led rate of £7,440 that is −£2,061k of funding a year. Taking out three quarters of the cost leaves −£515k, which added to its latest in-year balance of −£168k gives an annual position of −£684k, a deficit of 9% of its income. Its reserve of £531k would last about 0.8 years.

13.4 Where every school lands

Show code 
by_school_path %>%
  filter(year %in% c(min(yrs), max(yrs))) %>%
  mutate(year = factor(year),
         short = forcats::fct_reorder(short, gap_pct, min)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(gap_pct, short)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(aes(group = short), colour = "grey75", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = year), size = 3.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(c("#1f3b57", "#d95f02"),
                                        c(min(yrs), max(yrs))),
                      name = "Intake year") +
  labs(x = "Annual surplus or deficit, share of income", y = NULL,
       title = sprintf("%d schools in deficit on the 2026 intake, %d on the 2035 one",
                       o26$in_deficit,
                       money_path$in_deficit[money_path$year == max(yrs) & money_path$shed == SHED]),
       subtitle = sprintf("Steady-state roll; %.0f%% of lost funding taken out of costs", 100 * SHED)) +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top")

The ordering is not the ordering of intakes. King’s gains pupils against its funded roll and starts from a surplus; Cardinal Newman fills completely and is still the deepest in deficit, because its latest accounts already show a deficit of £1,740k a year. The model’s intakes decide the change; the accounts decide the starting point, and for several schools the starting point is most of the story.

13.5 Over time, and under the cost assumption

Show code 
money_path %>%
  mutate(shed = factor(sprintf("%.0f%% of lost funding cut from costs", 100 * shed),
                       levels = sprintf("%.0f%% of lost funding cut from costs",
                                        100 * c(0.9, 0.75, 0.5)))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(year, city_gap / 1e6, colour = shed)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey45") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#9aa5b1", "#1f3b57", "#d95f02"), name = NULL) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = function(x) ifelse(x < 0, sprintf("−£%.0fm", -x), sprintf("£%.0fm", x))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = yrs[yrs %% 2 == 0]) +
  labs(x = "Intake year on the slider", y = "All ten schools, per year",
       title = "The falling cohort turns into money only as fast as costs fail to follow it",
       subtitle = "Steady-state roll at each year's modelled intake, council priorities, today's map") +
  theme_bh() + theme(legend.position = "top", legend.direction = "vertical",
                     legend.justification = "left")

If every pound lost were a pound of cost cut (\(s = 1\)), the cohort decline would cost nothing and the city’s position would simply be the sum of today’s balances, −£474k. Even at 90% the city’s schools end 2035 at −£2,540k a year. At the simulator’s setting it is −£5,639k, and −£10,804k if schools can only cut half of what they lose. The assumption moves the answer more than most of the policy levers do, which is why the app states it on its money chart.

13.6 The model’s error, in pounds

The money table is only as good as the intakes behind it, and the closing section (§15) shows where the model’s intakes are wrong. Replacing the modelled 2026 intakes with the offers the council actually made isolates that:

Overdrawn and in deficit in this run — the ones a council acts on first 2: Hove Park, Cardinal Newman

13.8 What to be careful about

  • It is a steady state, not a budget. No pay award, no inflation, no energy prices, no capital receipts, no change in the funding formula. All in today’s money.
  • One year of accounts is the baseline. A school with one bad year carries it forward indefinitely; so does a school with one good one.
  • Sixth forms are outside it. Four schools have one. Their income includes post-16 funding, so a deficit as a share of income is flattered for them, and nothing in the model moves their sixth-form rolls.
  • The same cost assumption for everyone. A school with 91% of its income in staff costs cannot shed cost as easily as one at 68%, and the model treats them alike.
  • Patcham is overdrawn but in surplus. Its reserve is negative and its in-year balance positive, so it counts as having no years of reserve left while recovering. The app says “overdrawn” rather than printing a number that would mean the opposite.

13.9 Questions this raises

  1. Should the cost assumption vary by school, with staff share as the obvious first candidate?
  2. Should the roll move year by year, as a cohort model, rather than jumping to its steady state?
  3. Should the simulator rebase each school to its actual offers, as the open model does, and show only the change a scenario makes?

14 Scenarios: which runs, and how to read them

Everything so far has been one run of the model. The strategic view’s conclusions come from comparing many. This section says which runs those are, how they were chosen, what each is scored on, and — most importantly — how to read the difference between two of them.

14.1 What a scenario is

A scenario is a set of control settings and nothing more: a catchment map, a site for Longhill, some admission numbers, perhaps an attractiveness multiplier or a change to the admission rules, and a year. It is applied on top of the baseline, the model is run from step 1 (§11), and the outcomes are read off. No scenario changes a fitted parameter, and no scenario is a separate model.

Scenarios live in two places.

  • The simulator’s presets — 13 starting points, each a question rather than an answer, which a user then moves the controls away from.
  • The strategic view’s option set — 29 options in 7 groups, each run in 2026, 2030, 2035, which is 87 runs in all. Every recommendation in the strategic view rests on this table.

14.2 How the option set was chosen

The rule was levers the council actually holds: the admission numbers of the six community schools, the catchment map, Longhill’s site, and the oversubscription priorities. Options that need a decision from a school the council does not run are kept in a group of their own, so a reader can see at once which results the council could deliver by itself.

Show code 
co_runs %>%
  filter(year == min(year)) %>%
  group_by(group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), options = paste(short, collapse = "; "), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(group) %>%
  transmute(Group = as.character(group), Options = n, `What they are` = options) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrl")
The strategic view’s option set, by group.
Group Options What they are
Baseline 1 Today
Keep Longhill open 10 Longhill 150; Longhill 120; Longhill 150, 1.5× as wanted; Central schools trimmed; Central schools trimmed hard; Whitehawk back to Longhill; Whitehawk back, Longhill 150; Whitehawk back, central trims; Pre-2024 catchments; Longhill to Elm Grove, map redrawn
Access and segregation 6 Power-diagram catchments; Power diagram, Longhill 150; No priority 6; Priority 6 at 20%; An equal chance for all; CoMArt reopened
Fit the system 2 Community schools shrunk; Every school shrunk
Asks of schools the council does not run 3 Cardinal Newman 300; Cardinal Newman 270, King’s 150; Two academies cut
Packages 6 Package A; Package B; Package C; Package D; Package E; Package F
Counterfactual 1 Longhill closed

Three of those groups need a word.

  • Packages combine single levers, because the questions the council faces are not one lever at a time. Each package is named for what it adds to an earlier one, so their differences can be traced.
  • “Longhill closed” is a counterfactual, not a recommendation. It is there so every other option can be read against the alternative the council is actually weighing.
  • “Fit the system” cuts places to the 2035 cohort plus a margin (1,920 places in all). It answers how much of the empty-place problem is simply too many places, whatever else is done.

14.3 What every run is scored on

Each run is scored on every priority at once, so no option can look good by being measured on only the thing it was designed to fix.

14.4 How to read a scenario

Seven rules, each learned the hard way during this work.

1. Compare in the same year. The cohort falls by about a fifth between 2026 and 2035, and that alone changes every measure. An option in 2035 is read against today’s configuration in 2035 — the do-nothing case — never against today’s numbers in 2026. The grey line in the chart above is always the same-year baseline.

2. A ceiling that does not bind does nothing. Cutting Longhill to 150 or to 120 leaves every measure except empty places exactly where it was in 2030, because the model gives Longhill 70 children and neither number is reached: empty places fall from 583 to 523 and 493, and nothing else moves. An admission number only matters to the schools that fill.

3. Read the measure the option was designed to change, then all the others. Trimming the central schools (Stringer to 300, Varndean to 270, Blatchington Mill to 300, Longhill to 150) was meant to send children to Longhill. In 2030 Longhill’s intake under the option is 70.4 against 69.8 today — it barely moves. What the option does instead is cut 150 empty places and roughly double the children displaced, from 3 to 5. Refused children go to the schools with room that their catchment names second (§10), and Longhill is rarely that school.

4. Small differences in the segregation index are not findings. The Gorard index runs from 0.091 to 0.148 across the whole option set in 2030. §12 showed that re-measuring the same scenario moved it by about 0.01 and changed its sign. A difference smaller than that between two options should be read as “no clear difference”.

5. Know which results rest on held-fixed parameters. Every option keeps the fitted attractiveness, catchment terms and disadvantage pulls (§11). That is safe for an admission-number change and much less safe for a relocation or a reopening, where a school’s relationship with its families plainly changes. Moving Longhill to Elm Grove takes the deprived-journey gap from 3.7 to 0.4 minutes — a result about journeys, which the model measures directly — and the Gorard index from 0.106 to 0.140, a result that depends on Longhill’s fitted pull on disadvantaged children travelling with it to a new site.

6. A slider away from 1 is a question, not a forecast. “Longhill 1.5 times as wanted” does not say anything will make it so; it says what would follow if something did. Package B is Package A with that assumption added, and should be read as “Package A, if it also works”.

7. 2035 is an extrapolation, and the money is a steady state. The cohort projection runs out before 2035 and is extended (§2.7), and every money figure is the position a school converges on if the configuration is held (§13). The 2035 column is the direction of travel, not a plan.

14.5 A worked comparison

Show code 
ids <- c("today", "whitehawk", "elm", "package_f", "close_lh")
co_runs %>%
  filter(year == 2030, id %in% ids) %>%
  mutate(id = factor(id, ids)) %>% arrange(id) %>%
  transmute(Option = short,
            `Longhill intake` = ifelse(is.na(lh_intake), "—", sprintf("%.0f", lh_intake)),
            `Empty places` = fmt_n(round(empty)),
            `Community schools in deficit` = comm_in_deficit,
            `City position` = sprintf("−£%.1fm", -city_gap / 1e6),
            Gorard = sprintf("%.3f", gorard),
            `Deprived-journey gap` = sprintf("%.1f min", dep_gap),
            Displaced = sprintf("%.0f", displaced)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lrrrrrrr")
Four options against today’s configuration in 2030, on the measures the strategic view’s recommendation turns on.
Option Longhill intake Empty places Community schools in deficit City position Gorard Deprived-journey gap Displaced
Today 70 583 6 −£4.5m 0.106 3.7 min 3
Whitehawk back to Longhill 85 584 6 −£4.5m 0.116 3.4 min 0
Longhill to Elm Grove, map redrawn 86 528 6 −£4.5m 0.140 0.4 min 3
Package F 91 408 6 −£4.4m 0.138 0.5 min 3
Longhill closed — 386 4 −£3.1m 0.091 4.4 min 3

Read with the rules above:

  • Whitehawk back to Longhill raises Longhill’s intake by 15 children and cuts displacement to 0, and raises the Gorard index by 0.010 — about the size of the re-measurement effect in §12, so the segregation direction is the least secure part of the result.
  • Elm Grove — alone, or inside Package F — is the only change that nearly closes the deprived-journey gap. That is a journey result and it is the most robust thing in the table. Its segregation figure is the least robust (rule 5).
  • Package F adds the asks of the academies and faith schools to the move. Its gains over Elm Grove alone are in empty places, and they depend on decisions the council cannot make (the group rule).
  • Longhill closed has the fewest community schools in deficit and the lowest Gorard index — and the longest journeys of the five. It is on the table so the others can be judged against it, not because the model recommends it.

14.6 The simulator’s presets

Show code 
tibble(Preset = names(inp$presets),
       `What it sets` = vapply(inp$presets, function(p) p$note, "")) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "ll")
The starting points offered in the simulator. Each is a set of overrides on Today; the user moves the controls from there.
Preset What it sets
Today The city as it stands: today’s admission numbers, today’s catchments, Longhill at Ovingdean, and the council’s 2026/27 admission priorities.
Do nothing until 2035 Everything held as it is, with the cohort ten years smaller. This is the do-nothing case the rest of the document describes.
Longhill to Elm Grove, PAN 150 The relocation, at the reduced admission number, behind the catchments drawn for it.
Hove Park on one site Hove Park teaches Year 7 at the Valley Campus on Hangleton Way, 1.65 km west of the Nevill Road site its address gives. The council has given notice to close the Valley Campus on 31 August 2028. This runs the first year of the consolidated school; switch Hove Park’s Year 7 site to the Valley Campus to see the same year as it would have been. The total barely moves. Where the children come from does: at Hangleton Way the school draws far more of Hangleton & Knoll and Portslade, and much less of Westdene, Hove Park ward and Poets’ Corner.
Redraw for balance The power diagram, which spreads disadvantage most evenly of the designs tested, with everything else as it is.
Shrink the system to fit Total places cut to 1,920, about 5% above the 2035 cohort of 1,835, and shared out in proportion to today’s admission numbers. Move the total or any school from there.
Make the catchment count Everything as it is, but living in a catchment weighs far more heavily on the choice than families currently behave as though it does. This is the other way to fill a school, and it needs nothing from the school itself.
Make Longhill wanted Longhill’s attractiveness lifted to Dorothy Stringer’s, everything else unchanged. The question is what it takes, and who loses the children.
Everyone has the same chance Today’s city with no oversubscription priorities: every applicant to a full school has the same chance, which is the model section 7 of the strategic view publishes. Compare the Catchments and Fairness tabs with Today, which runs the council’s 2026/27 priorities.
The council’s first proposal: 20% open The open-admissions priority as the council first consulted on it, at 20% of places rather than the 5% it settled on after objections from the six community schools. Watch displacement in the two dual catchments.
The 2027/28 rules: Targeted FSM The 2027/28 arrangements: the FSM priority narrowed to Targeted FSM, which the council puts at about 56% of currently eligible children. Everything else as in 2026/27.
CoMArt re-opened: three small eastern schools CoMArt, closed in 2005, open again on its East Brighton site with 150 places, sharing Longhill’s catchment, and Brighton Aldridge and Longhill both cut to 150. Watch segregation, journeys, and whether the central schools still fill.
CoMArt re-opened, and Stringer to 300 The same three small eastern schools, with Dorothy Stringer’s admission number cut from 330 to 300. Does Stringer still fill, and where do the children go?

14.8 What to be careful about

  • The option set is a choice. It covers the levers the council holds and some it does not, but it is not every configuration of them. Something good may lie between two rows.
  • Every run is a mean. The lottery is averaged (§9), so no option shows how much a real round could differ from its row.
  • The measures are not weighted. The chart and the tables show every measure side by side on purpose. The strategic view weighs them, and says how; this guide does not.
  • Options are run on today’s fitted behaviour. A scenario that changes how families see a school — a new building, a new head, a relocation — changes the thing the model holds fixed.

14.9 Questions this raises

  1. Should the option set be searched rather than listed — every combination of admission numbers the council could set, scored and filtered?
  2. Should each option carry an uncertainty band from the lottery and from the fitted parameters, so rule 4 can be applied by the reader rather than by judgement?
  3. Should the relocation and reopening options be re-run with the disadvantage pull and attractiveness allowed to vary over a plausible range, since those are the results that lean on them most?

15 The matrix, filled in

15.1 The example from §1, with numbers in it

Section 1 set out the shape of the model for four neighbourhoods and four schools and left the interior empty. Every term since has filled in one part of it. Here it is complete, for 2026:

Show code 
mk <- function(z, s) {
  r <- end_cells %>% filter(zone == z, name == s)
  if (!nrow(r)) return("—")
  sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", r$wanted, r$offered)
}
data.frame(
  Neighbourhood = c(sub("[|].*$", "", end_z), "$W_j$"),
  `Dorothy Stringer` = c(unname(vapply(end_z, mk, "", s = end_s[1])), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[end_s[1]]])),
  Varndean = c(unname(vapply(end_z, mk, "", s = end_s[2])), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[end_s[2]]])),
  Longhill = c(unname(vapply(end_z, mk, "", s = end_s[3])), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[end_s[3]]])),
  `Cardinal Newman` = c(unname(vapply(end_z, mk, "", s = end_s[4])), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[end_s[4]]])),
  `$A_i$` = c(sprintf("%.2f", end_A$A[match(end_z, end_A$zone)]), ""),
  `$O_i$ (2026)` = c(sprintf("%.1f", ex_zones$Oi), ""),
  check.names = FALSE) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lccccrr")
The four largest neighbourhoods and four of the schools, as the model leaves them. Each cell is children wanting that school, with what they are offered after the ceiling in brackets. The rows do not sum to \(O_i\) here because six other destinations are off the right-hand side of the table.
Neighbourhood Dorothy Stringer Varndean Longhill Cardinal Newman \(A_i\) \(O_i\) (2026)
E01016901 7.6 (12.5) 20.7 (15.6) 0.0 (0.0) 0.8 (0.6) 2.58 29.8
E01016880 0.2 (0.2) 0.3 (0.1) 0.0 (0.0) 2.0 (1.7) 7.37 27.1
E01016979 0.4 (0.3) 0.5 (0.0) 0.0 (0.0) 4.5 (3.8) 11.75 25.5
E01016997 0.4 (0.3) 0.9 (0.0) 0.0 (0.0) 4.3 (3.6) 18.64 24.3
\(W_j\) 0.55 1.03 0.10 3.27

Read one row and the whole model is in it. The neighbourhood’s children (\(O_i\), §2) are divided between schools in proportion to each school’s pull — its attractiveness (\(W_j\), §3) discounted by the journey (\(c_{ij}\), §4; \(\beta\), §5), multiplied up if the neighbourhood is in its catchment (\(\gamma_h\), §6) and nudged by how crowded it is (\(C_j\), \(\delta\), §7) — with \(A_i\) (§8) set so the row places every child. Then the admission numbers bind (§9) and the children who are refused are re-offered somewhere else (§10), which is why the two numbers in a cell differ.

The model sends too few children to the two Aldridge academies and too many to Hove Park and Patcham. That is one story, not four: the model has no term for a school’s reputation changing, and these are the schools whose intakes have moved most in recent rounds. §3’s note on time is the place that gap is discussed.

Four things in that table are fitted to observed behaviour (\(W_j\), \(\gamma_h\), \(\delta\), the exclusivity shares), one is fixed by hand (\(\beta\)), one is solved to match a published total (FSM take-up), and everything else is either measured or published. That is the honest division, and it is worth carrying into any reading of a scenario: the further a scenario moves from the city as it is, the more weight falls on the four fitted quantities and the less on the published ones.

15.4 If a number looks wrong

The symptom Where to look first
A neighbourhood has too many or too few children §2: the zone’s postcode count and its split across catchments
A school is more or less wanted than expected §3: its fitted \(W_j\), and whether the slider is at 1
A journey looks implausible §4: the walk cap and the distance fallback
Everyone goes to their nearest school §5: \(\beta\), and §6: the catchment term
A school fills that should not §10: what is being re-offered to it, and from where
The city total does not match the council’s §2.6: the projection and the state-sector share
An out-of-city school takes too many §8: the decay on straight-line kilometres
The FSM tiers look too large §9: siblings sit inside the catchment tier

15.5 Following a number back

Every figure in the strategic view comes from one of the runs described in §14, which is the model of §2 to §10 with the disadvantage layer of §12 and the money of §13 read off the result. It should now be possible to follow any number back through these sections to a published source.

Source Code
---
title: "The model, stage by stage"
subtitle: "A technical guide for checking each element"
author: "Adam Dennett, UCL Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis"
date: today
abstract: |
  This document takes the model the simulator runs and opens it up one
  element at a time. Each section states what a term is, where its data
  comes from, exactly how it is computed, what it looks like for a worked
  example, the checks that can be run against it, and what it assumes. It
  is written to be audited: every number is produced by the code in this
  repository, and every step should be reproducible by hand.
---

```{r setup}
#| include: false
source(here::here("R", "00_core.R"))
library(scales)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(dev = "ragg_png", dpi = 150)

oi  <- bh_data("open_inputs.rds")
mt  <- bh_data("model_terms.rds")
inp <- readRDS(here::here("app", "data", "sim_inputs.rds"))
z   <- oi$zones
zc  <- z %>% filter(area != "Expansion area")
dem <- inp$demand
cal <- mt$calibrated
rc  <- bh_data("reception_cohort.rds")
acc <- bh_data("accessibility.rds")

# The simulator's own engine, so the guide can run the model it describes.
source(here::here("app", "R", "model.R"))
source(here::here("app", "R", "outcomes.R"))

# The state-sector share is a single constant in the open bundle's build.
# It is recovered here from the projection rather than retyped, so this
# document cannot drift from the number the model used.
dem_raw <- readr::read_csv(here::here("data", "open_demand_projection.csv"),
                           show_col_types = FALSE)
STATE_SHARE <- with(dem_raw[dem_raw$area == "Brighton & Hove" &
                              dem_raw$entry_year == 2026, ],
                    state_demand / children)
W5 <- cal$W / mean(cal$W)
```

# What this document is

The simulator runs one model. Everything in the strategic view, and every
scenario in it, is that model with different settings. This guide takes
it apart in the order the model is written, so that each piece can be
checked on its own.

$$
T_{ij}^{\,y} \;=\; A_i^{\,y}\, O_i^{\,y}\, W_j\, c_{ij}^{-\beta}\,
e^{\gamma_{h(i)} \cdot \mathbb{1}[\,i \in \text{catchment}(j)\,]}\, C_j^{\delta},
\qquad
A_i^{\,y} = \frac{1}{\sum_k W_k\, c_{ik}^{-\beta}\, e^{\gamma_{h(i)} \mathbb{1}[\cdot]}\, C_k^{\delta}}
$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Section |
|:--|:--|:--|
| $T_{ij}$ | children from neighbourhood $i$ modelled as attending school $j$ | the interior of the matrix |
| $O_i$ | children in neighbourhood $i$ entering Year 7 | §2 |
| $W_j$ | how attractive school $j$ is, net of where it stands | §3 |
| $c_{ij}$ | routed walk-and-bus journey time from $i$ to $j$ | §4 |
| $\beta$ | distance decay | §5 |
| $\gamma_h$ | catchment term, fitted for each catchment $h$ | §6 |
| $C_j$, $\delta$ | competing destinations | §7 |
| $A_i$ | balancing factor: every neighbourhood places all of its children | §8 |
| $y$ | entry year, carried as a superscript | §2.7 |

Two further stages are applied to the $T_{ij}$ this produces: the
admission-number ceiling with the council's oversubscription priorities
(§9), and the re-offering of the children it refuses (§10).

::: {.callout-note}

## The year is the only dynamic element, and it enters in one place

Nothing in the equation carries a time subscript except $O_i$. Journey
times, attractiveness, catchment terms and admission numbers are all held
at a single point in time, and the year chosen on the simulator's slider
changes only the **size** of each neighbourhood's cohort (§2.7). Whether
that is the right treatment — and what an explicit time dimension would
have to carry — is a question this guide returns to once the static terms
are set out.
:::

```{r matrix-blank}
#| tbl-cap: "The shape of the model, for four neighbourhoods and four schools. Sections 2 and 3 fill in the two margins shown; the rest follow, and the interior cells come last."
ex_zones <- zc %>% arrange(desc(Oi)) %>% slice(1:4)
sch4 <- c("Dorothy Stringer School", "Varndean School",
          "Longhill High School", "Cardinal Newman Catholic School")
data.frame(
  Neighbourhood = c(sub("[|].*$", "", ex_zones$zone), "$W_j$"),
  `Dorothy Stringer` = c(rep("$T_{ij}$", 4), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[1]]])),
  Varndean = c(rep("$T_{ij}$", 4), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[2]]])),
  Longhill = c(rep("$T_{ij}$", 4), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[3]]])),
  `Cardinal Newman` = c(rep("$T_{ij}$", 4), sprintf("%.2f", W5[[sch4[4]]])),
  `$A_i$` = c(rep("?", 4), ""),
  `$O_i$ (2026)` = c(sprintf("%.1f", ex_zones$Oi), ""),
  check.names = FALSE) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "lccccrr")
```

The interior of that matrix is what the model produces. The margins are
what it is given, or what it fits. $O_i$ is the one margin that is a
count of real people, and it is where this guide starts.

# $O_i$: the children in each neighbourhood {#sec-oi}

## What it is

$O_i$ is the number of children living in zone $i$ who will enter Year 7
at a **state** secondary school in the year being modelled. The model is
production-constrained on it, which means that whatever else happens,

$$\sum_j T_{ij} = O_i \quad \text{for every } i.$$

Every child is placed somewhere. Nothing is created and nothing is lost,
which is why $O_i$ has to be right before anything else can be.

## What a zone is

A zone is **an LSOA cut by catchment**, keyed as
`LSOA | pre-2024 catchment | current catchment`. The city has
`r fmt_n(nrow(zc))` zones drawn from `r fmt_n(n_distinct(zc$lsoa))`
LSOAs.

The cut exists because the 2024 boundary change runs *through* LSOAs.
Assigning a whole LSOA to whichever catchment contains its centroid would
register only a fraction of the children the redraw actually moves. So
every postcode in the ONS Postcode Directory is assigned a catchment on
each of the two maps by point-in-polygon, and the LSOA is split
accordingly. Carrying **both** maps in the key means the two regimes sit
on identical geography and can be compared without rebuilding anything.

```{r zone-example}
#| tbl-cap: "Two LSOAs on the Longhill / Stringer-Varndean boundary, each split into two zones: the same neighbourhood, a different catchment on the current map."
z %>%
  filter(lsoa %in% c("E01016862", "E01016863")) %>%
  transmute(Zone = zone, LSOA = lsoa, `Pre-2024` = catch_pre2024,
            `Current map` = catch_optionZ, Postcodes = n_pcd,
            `$O_i$ (2026)` = sprintf("%.1f", Oi)) %>%
  knitr::kable(align = "llllrr")
```

## Where the numbers come from {#sec-oi-sources}

| Input | Source | What it supplies |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Ward population by single year of age, mid-2022 | [ONS ward-level mid-year population estimates](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/datasets/wardlevelmidyearpopulationestimatesexperimental) (`sapewardstablefinal.xlsx`) | how many children of each age live in each ward |
| LSOA population by single year of age | [ONS lower super output area mid-year population estimates](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/populationandmigration/populationestimates/datasets/lowersuperoutputareamidyearpopulationestimates) (`lsoa_age_11_props_totals.xlsx`) | how a ward's children divide between its LSOAs |
| Postcode directory, February 2024 | [ONS Postcode Directory, ONS Open Geography Portal](https://geoportal.statistics.gov.uk/) | which ward and LSOA each postcode is in |
| Catchment boundaries | [Brighton & Hove City Council, school admissions](https://www.brighton-hove.gov.uk/schools-and-learning/school-admissions) — the option Z map in force from 2026 entry, and the map it replaced | the catchment half of the zone key |
| Year 7 offers, 2024 | [Allocation factsheet, Year 7 places September 2024](https://www.brighton-hove.gov.uk/schools-and-learning/school-policies-reports-strategies-and-other-documents/allocation-factsheet-year-7-places-september-2024) | the state-sector share |
| LSOA boundaries | [ONS Open Geography Portal](https://geoportal.statistics.gov.uk/) | drawing, and joining the age data to zones |

None of it is pupil-level. The smallest thing any of these sources
describes is a postcode count or an LSOA age band.

## How $O_i$ is built, step by step

The code is `public/R/01_open_inputs.R` in the private bundle, sections
1b and 1c. Its result travels to the simulator as `data/open_inputs.rds`.

**Step 1 — ages become entry years.** A child aged $a$ in the mid-2022
estimates enters Year 7 in $2022 + (11 - a)$. Ages 0 to 11 therefore give
entry years 2022 to 2033, every one of them children ONS has already
counted rather than births anyone has projected.

**Step 2 — two extrapolated years.** Children entering in 2034 and 2035
were not born when the mid-2022 estimate was taken. They are a linear
continuation of the five most recent observed cohorts, 2029 to 2033, and
are flagged as extrapolated wherever they appear.

**Step 3 — resident children become state-sector demand.** Not every
resident child takes a state Year 7 place: some go to independent
schools, some leave the city. A single constant carries that:

$$\text{state share} \;=\; \frac{\text{Year 7 offers made, 2024}}{\text{resident children, 2024 entry}} \;=\; `r sprintf("%.3f", STATE_SHARE)`$$

taken from the council's published offer total against the ONS cohort of
the same year.

**Step 4 — a ward is divided between its zones.** ONS publishes the age
detail at ward level, so each ward's children are shared out between the
zones in it. The weight for a zone is its LSOA's age-11 population share,
divided between the zones that LSOA is cut into by their postcode counts:

$$u_i \;=\; \underbrace{p_{\ell(i)}}_{\text{LSOA age-11 share}} \times
\underbrace{\frac{n_i}{\sum_{k \in \ell(i)} n_k}}_{\text{postcodes in this zone}},
\qquad
O_i^{\,2026} \;=\; \text{ward children}_{w(i)} \times \frac{u_i}{\sum_{k \in w(i)} u_k} \times \text{state share}$$

where $\ell(i)$ is the zone's LSOA, $w(i)$ its ward and $n_i$ its
postcode count. `r fmt_n(sum(!is.na(z$prop)))` of the `r fmt_n(nrow(z))`
zones use the ONS age share; the `r fmt_n(sum(is.na(z$prop)))` in the
expansion area outside the city fall back to postcode counts alone.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}

## Why not divide a ward by postcode count

Splitting a ward's children by how many postcodes each LSOA holds assumes
every postcode contains the same number of eleven-year-olds. Family
housing, student housing and retirement housing differ enormously on
that, and the difference runs along exactly the lines catchment
